Labelled ‘Lios Caointe’ on Robinson’s map (1977) – a name deriving from a local tradition of fairy songs being heard here (Westropp 1915, 256). Listed as ‘Ringfort’ in the RMP (1996). ay have led to another chamber. This may be the chamber reported by Cooke (1851, 297). The current entrance is at the ENE end of the chamber (1.2m) where a lintel has been displaced; this may be an original entrance or a creep. In Cooke’s time, two chambers connected by a creep were accessible. The second was of similar dimension to the first and ran perpendicular. He also reported the find of a ‘fairy millstone’, a round stone an inch and a half in diameter. He did not note whether it was perforated, but it is likely to have been a spindle whorl.  Compiled by: Mary Tunney and Ros Ó Maoldúin  Date of upload: 15 December 2020

A rough wall of close-set/contiguous large boulders encircles the roughly circular, flat summit of the knoll. On a prominent steep hill, now planted with coniferous forest, overlooking an extensive multiperiod field system (CL009-001001-) to the N. Hachured and named 'Lissateeaun' on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Labelled as 'Lios an tSidheáin' on Robinson's (1977) map - a name translated as 'Fairy Hill' in the OS Letters (1839) (Comber 1997, 71). This subtriangular rath (36.7m E-W; 27m N-S) is defined by a steep scarp from SW-SE and by a deep round-bottomed fosse (Wth 4-6m) along the S side. The fosse is 7m below the level of the summit of the platform and 2m below the surrounding ground level. The scarp may be largely natural. Wes

On a shelf near the SE foot of a steep ridge overlooking a narrow valley to the E, and a nearby pond on lower ground to the W. Hachured and labelled ‘Lishaghaun’ on both the first (1842) and Cassini (1920) editions of the OS 6-inch map. Labelled ‘Liosachán’ on Robinson’s map of the Burren (1977). Listed as ‘Enclosure’ in the RMP (1996). This circular cashel (diams. 25.8m E–W; 25.5m N–S) is defined by a double-faced dry-stone wall (Wth at N 3m; int. H 0.3–0.9m; ext. H 0.3–1m) with a possible clay core. The outer wall-face is visible intermittently while the inner wall-face is traceable from NW–N. A later wall is built over the cashel wall from SSE–S

In pasture. Roughly circular area (diam. c. 30m) enclosed by low earthen bank (int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.4m) S->N; linear earthen stone-faced field boundary to NE; earthen stone-faced field boundary to SE, which curves and most likely incorporates original earthen bank. Bank and interior planted with mature coniferous trees. Locally known as fairy fort.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.  Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

In pasture, on N-facing slope. Depicted as tree ring on 1842 OS 6-inch map. No visible surface trace. According to local information, an old man living in the area pointed to a clump of furze here and said that bad luck would come to any one who ploughed it.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.  Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

Bowman (1934, 718) records levelled, single-ramparted, fort (diam. c. 25yd) on Eugene Linehan's land 'called Lissafooka (Lios an Phuca) - fort of the ghost'. Exact location not known.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.  Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

Bowman (1934, 53) records levelled, single-ramparted fort (diam. c. 43yd) in J. O'Hanlon's land; field called 'Pairc a Phuca'. Exact location not known.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 4: North Cork' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2000). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.  Date of upload/revision: 14 January 2009

Danes Fort' on a 1775 map (no. 26) by B. Scalé (private collection). A roughly circular area (diam. c. 33m N-S; c. 25m E-W) defined by a low grass-covered rise. A shallow depression outside the low rise appears to indicate the former presence of a fosse along the E and W sectors. A field boundary running roughly NE-SW to the SE-S of the rath curves to respect it. The rath is locally known as the 'fairy fort' and the field in which it stands is known as the 'Kill field'.  The above description is derived from 'The Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Volume 5' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 2009).  Date of upload: 22 December 2009

Mulcahy (1991, 32) records 'a small field called An Liosachán' in which was found a 'large number of subterranean chambers....the roofs of which had collapsed'. Tradition that one chamber was used as a forge at beginning of 19th century. Exact location not known.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cork. Not marked on any OS ed. Known locally as the site of a 'fairy fort' (local information). All that survives to indicate the possible presence of an enclosure here is a raised circular platform (diam. c. 25m) demarcated by the curve of a now disused laneway from SE-S-NW. The inner face of the laneway is bordered by a low narrow bank of earth and stone.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cavan' (Dublin: Sta

In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research. Date of upload/revision: 17 July 2007  Known locally as 'Fairy Haggard'. Small subcircular field (diam. c. 38m), stone wall at N recently levelled. Probably incorporates former enclosure.

There is no sign of the irregularly shaped 'Fort' shown on the 1st and 2nd editions of the OS 6-inch maps. The area is known as a 'fairy fort' and consists of ridges of rock outcrop in rough pasture. This topography would suggest a stone-built enclosure.  The above description was derived from the 'Archaeological Survey of County Donegal. A description of the field antiquities of the County from the Mesolithic Period to the 17th century.' Compiled by: Brian Lacey with Eamon Cody, Claire Cotter, Judy Cuppage, Noel Dunne, Vincent Hu

On a very prominent hill in otherwise gently undulating grassland. Known locally as the site of a 'fort' with a 'cave' (possible souterrain). No visible surface trace of either survives. According to local tradition, it is unlucky to till the field. The 'cave' is reputed to run to a another probable souterrain (GA046-028----), 2.5km to ENE.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).   Date of upload: 05 August 2010

On the summit of a ridge in undulating grassland. The poorly preserved remains of an enclosure (N-S c. 51m) which is cut from N to S by the Ballymoe-Ballinlough road. To W of the road, the arc of a bank survives from SW to NW. No visible surface trace survives to E. Known locally as a 'fairy fort'.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).   Date of upload: 05 August 2010

In grassland. Marked on 1st ed. of OS 6-inch map as an oval enclosure (c. 45m by c. 35m). By time of 3rd ed. (1920), its NE end appears to have been truncated by a field boundary. Though known locally as the site of a 'fairy fort', no visible surface trace survives.  The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).   Date of upload: 05 August 2010

On a hillock in undulating pastureland. This small circular enclosure (diam. 8.2m) is defined by a bank of earth and stone. Upright boulders mark an entrance gap (Wth 1.2m) at SE. The interior is obscured by  field-clearance rubble. Lynch Athy (1914, 136) recorded that the monument was known locally as ‘Lisheen na Shinawn ("fort of the fairy wind")’ and that it was said to be the burial place of a soldier. Classified by McCaffrey (1952, 138, no. 8a) as a ‘hut circle’. Possibly a barrow or a house site.   Compiled by: Galway Archaeological Survey, UCG  Date of upload: 30 July 2019

Some 80m to the E of a rath (GA108-051----). Known locally as 'Fairy Hill', this enclosure (18.7m E-W; 16.8m N-S), which is densely overgrown with trees and bramble, is defined by two banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank appears to be rectangular in plan while the outer bank appears to be more subcircular in outline.  Compiled by: Galway Archaeological Survey, UCG  Date of upload: 8 December 2017

According to local folklore collected from Lackbrooder School this was known locally as 'a Fairy Fort' (The Schools’ Collection, Volume 0450, Page 149; https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4713231/4709630/4760321).    Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien  Date of upload: 27 April 2022

Unlocated possible cashel described by Cuppage (1986, 229, no. 727) as follows; 'On a visit to this townland in 1949 the Co. Kerry Field Club visited 'a small caher with a large beehive-shaped hut outside the wall'. They also visited 2 sites which they described as 'liosacháns '. A drystone-built grave of 'average size' was discovered here on the W side of a field fence about 40 years ago (local information). There are conflicting reports as to whether it contained bones or not.   About a metre from the E side of the same field fence is a feature known locally as a 'liosachán'. This consists of a confused, stony area, c. 10.8m E-W x c. 13m N-S and c. 0.3 to .5m high, incorporating a single orthostat .5m high. Its classification and relationship to the grave are not known.  The above description is derived from J. Cuppage, ‘Corca Dhuibhne. Dingle Peninsula archaeological survey. Ballyferriter. Oidhreacht Chorca Dhuibhne’ (1986), no. 195. In certain instances the entrie

According to local information, this is referred to as the ‘fairy fort’.   Compiled by: Alison McQueen and Vera Rahilly   Date of upload: 8 September 2014

Another fort called An Liosachán was apparently located in the neighbouring townland of Ballintemple (KE052-017----), but this latter example seems to have been too small to classify as a ringfort. This souterrain, not marked on the OS maps, is located on top of an oval-shaped hillock whose flat upper surface measures 30m NW-SE x 17.5m NE-SW. The hillock is bounded on its N side by a field wall while it is defined by a low earthen bank at W; its sides are covered in a layer of dense vegetation. This site may be the 'Liosachán' referred to by Ó Cíobháin (1984b, 64). The E facing lintelled entrance to the souterrain, .75m x .75m, leads into a passage which is aligned N-S and measures at least 3.9m long. Its N end is blocked with collapse and it is not clear if it originally continued further in this direction. The passage is .9m wide and 1.35m in height. According to O'Kelly (1969, 8) the rath of Doorath was located, 'on the now wooded hillpoint at 550' overlooking BallyKeeffe Hill quarry, where Johnnie Murphy maintained he used to hear the fairy fiddle music'. The enclosure is not visible on satellite imagery (Digitalglobe and Google Earth, viewed 26 May 2021) in the area N of Ballykeefe Wood. The precise location of the enclosure is unknown.  Compiled by: Jean Farrelly  Date of upload: 26 May 2021

Located on a rise at the bottom of the E-facing slope of a drumlin. It is depicted as a circular enclosure with trees on the perimeter on the 1835 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described as ‘Sheean Fort’ – the Fairies Fort, and it is depicted as a D-shaped hachured feature with the same name but truncated by an ENE-WSW field bank at N on the 1945 revision. This is a slightly raised circular area (diam. c. 24m E-W) defined by a slight scarp (H 0.2m) and slightly truncated by the field bank at N. Indicated on the 1st (1840) ed. 6-inch OS map as an oval area (dims. c. 47m NW-SE; c. 30m NE-SW). By the 2nd (1954) ed. the S-W-N side is indicated defined by scarp (dims. at top c. 38m NW-SE) and an outer fosse while the E side is not indicated, though there is a circular hollow (diam. c. 20m) shown in the E quadrant. The monument has been incorporated into the 15th green which is known as the ‘Fairy hole’. It has been landscaped to form a manicured, oval-shaped platform (dims. 34m N-S; 21.5m) defined by scarp (H 1.5m; Wth 6m) and there is a hollow immediately to the E.  Compiled by: Jean Farrelly  Date of upload: 12 December 2012

Marked faintly as subcircular area (diam. c. 45m) described as a fairy rath only on the 1940 ed. of the OS 6-inch map. It is depicted with a fragment of surviving bank at SE within a small rectangular field. It is situated towards the bottom of an E-facing slope in the valley of the N-S River Bann with the stream c. 170m to the E.
